Context. We run a small cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab) with an AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2.5k, 1.5 kg payload, roughly 15 N of gripping force, wrist joint J5 limited to plus or minus 70 degrees, so no straight-down grasps near the table), SO-101 leader/follower arms, Raspberry Pi 5 wrist and fixed cameras, AprilTags, and Bambu Lab printers (two A1 mini bed-slingers with 180 mm magnetic textured-PEI plates, and an H2D). Prints are sent remotely by an AI agent after a human approval, and the agent will not send a print until a camera frame shows the plate clear; today a person removes every part. We want the arm to clear plates (first for a batch of small toys on the A1 minis in December), and later to move printed specimens into mechanical tests inside closed design-print-test loops: 3D-printed tensegrity structures under drop or compression tests, and printed fixtures for our alloy and powder workflows. A previous literature answer claimed that no publication shows an arm unloading 3D printers inside a closed experimental loop; we believe Boston University's BEAR and MAMA BEAR systems (Gongora et al. 2020, Science Advances; Snapp et al. 2024, Nature Communications) contradict this, and we also know of SmartLab (2025), TeleopLab, and commercial plate-swapping systems such as Prusa's automatic sheet changer.

Question.
(1) Which academic and industrial systems use a robot arm (or other mechanism) to remove parts from FFF/FDM printers or swap build plates? For each: the removal method (flexing a magnetic spring-steel sheet, scraping or pushing, swapping the whole plate, tilting, ejection by the print head), the printers and arms used (especially any low-cost arms), measured success rates with trial counts, cycle times, failure modes (parts stuck when warm, small or tall parts tipping, adhesion changes with plate wear), and the bed temperature or cool-down conditions that make release reliable.
(2) Closed-loop design-print-test systems with robotic specimen handling (BEAR and MAMA BEAR, SmartLab, and any others): what the arm does, how specimens reach testing machines (universal testers, compression, impact or drop rigs), throughput, uptime, human interventions or failure rates reported, and the limitations and future work their authors state.
(3) Camera-based print monitoring and verification relevant to a robot cell: detecting print failures (detachment, spaghetti, warping, layer shift) with low-cost cameras and reported accuracy; checking that the plate is clear before the next print; and automatic measurement of printed specimens (dimensions, mass, defects) before testing.
(4) Print farms with robotic tending: published throughput, uptime, human hours per print and cost per part, versus manual farms.
(5) Remote or cloud users who submit design-print-test jobs (for example BEAR's external-user pilots or teleoperated test labs): measured outcomes such as completion rate, turnaround and interventions.
(6) Given our arm's limits, which removal methods are feasible for small parts on a 180 mm bed-slinger, what forces are involved (adhesion force of PLA or PETG on textured PEI, sheet-flex force), and what is known about grasping irregular printed parts with a parallel gripper?

Prefer peer-reviewed sources from 2015 to 2026, and flag preprints, theses, and commercial or trade sources. For each claim give the DOI or URL and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.

(budzik2024possibilitiesofautomating pages 3-5, budzik2024possibilitiesofautomating pages 1-2) | Open MEX printers including Prusa MK3S-class equipment | Collaborative arm; model not reported in captured evidence | Proposed transfer to quality control; no specific mechanical test | No measured throughput, uptime, success rate, human-hours, or cost-per-part reported. | No numerical cool-down/release condition reported. | Conceptual architecture rather than a statistically validated farm trial; platform-transfer reliability, wear, and part-release failures were not quantified. |


*Table: Comparison of published and commercial mechanisms for FFF part removal, build-sheet handling, and robotic specimen transfer into mechanical tests. It distinguishes measured results from unreported metrics and flags non-peer-reviewed or commercial evidence.*

**BEAR / MAMA BEAR (Boston University).** The Bayesian Experimental Autonomous Researcher (BEAR), first reported in Gongora et al. 2020 (*Science Advances*, DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aaz1708), uses five dual-extruder MakerGear M3 FDM printers arranged within the working radius of a six-axis Universal Robots UR5e arm, a Sartorius CP225D scale, and an Instron 5965 universal testing machine (gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 1-2, gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 2-3). The expanded campaign (Snapp et al. 2024, *Nature Communications*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-48534-4) details the removal method: before each print, an arm-mounted camera checks whether the bed is clear; if cleaning is needed, the arm uses a scraper with up to ten retry attempts, taking a verification photo each time; if the bed remains dirty the printer is deactivated and an operator is notified (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 28-33). After printing, the bed is heated for TPE and TPU-1/2 (100 °C) to facilitate removal, or allowed to cool to 30 °C for PLA, PETG, Nylon, and TPU-3 (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 23-26). Failure modes include dirty beds, unsuccessful component grabs, misorientation, mass/height deviations >5%, severe print defects, insufficient strain data, and periodic need to replace worn polyimide tape and load new filament rolls (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 28-33). No explicit handling success-rate percentage was reported.

**FlexTrak automated sheet-flexing system (thesis, 2020).** This non-peer-reviewed student project describes a modular system for the Prusa i3 MK3 that elevates the magnetic spring-steel sheet off the bed (requiring approximately 15.48 N normal force to break magnetic retention, and 6.76 N horizontal pull), feeds it through a curved bending track using powered rollers, and uses passive scrapers to remove remaining debris (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 60-70, me2020increasing3dprinter pages 56-60). A decision-matrix comparison rated sheet flexing higher than disposable roll media (3.75 vs. 3.1) for reliability, modularity, and maintainability (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 52-56). Scraper-only removal was tested and found unreliable: it damaged small parts, retained parts on the blade, was limited to about 38% of the bed area (150 cm² maximum on a 400 cm² bed), required favorable part orientation and rafts, and produced visible scrape marks after 250 cycles (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 28-33, me2020increasing3dprinter pages 23-28). Print-head collision/ejection was also described, wherein modified G-code causes the print head to ram the part off; this requires no hardware modification but needs parts approximately 1 inch tall and becomes harder as contact area increases (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 28-33). Overnight, weekend, and full-spool reliability tests were planned but not quantitatively reported (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 1-7, me2020increasing3dprinter pages 7-9).

**ATCAM (Mazhari et al. 2021, *Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance*, DOI: 10.1007/s11665-021-06042-2).** This peer-reviewed system prints dynamic coupons on a Prusa MK3S and ejects them using an in-situ actuator (ISA) printed on the build surface; the toolhead pulls back the ISA, which releases stored energy through a 25.4 mm sphere to impact-eject each coupon toward a load cell (mazhari2021automatedtestingand pages 1-2, mazhari2021automatedtestingand pages 2-4, mazhari2021automatedtestingand pages 2-2). The actuator generates approximately 2 N of force, and the coupon base is designed with reduced contact area to lower adhesion. Each ISA was reused for 100 nondestructive ejection cycles, after which manual replacement was required (mazhari2021automatedtestingand pages 2-4). A total of 3,000 coupons were generated across three PLA feedstocks (mazhari2021automatedtestingand pages 4-5). No explicit ejection success rate was reported, but automated ejection was described as the most difficult engineering challenge (mazhari2021automatedtestingand pages 1-2).

**SmartLab (Yun et al. 2025, *Journal of Computational Design and Engineering*, DOI: 10.1093/jcde/qwaf034).** This peer-reviewed system uses a San Robotics M1013 arm on a Syscon Scorpion A-100 mobile base. After printing, the robot removes the entire printer bed with a suction gripper, measures the specimen with a wrist camera, changes to a finger gripper via a pneumatic gripper changer, detaches the specimen, and places it on a rack for downstream measurement and testing (yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 6-7, yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 5-6). No bed temperature or cool-down protocol was specified in the retrieved evidence.

**Commercial systems.** Prusa Research's automated farm system (Prusa Pro AFS) and other commercial plate-swapping solutions (e.g., Bambu Lab conveyor concepts) exist as trade products, but **no peer-reviewed trial counts, success rates, failure-mode studies, or comparative cost analyses were located.** These should be treated as commercial/trade sources only.

### (2) Closed-Loop Design-Print-Test Systems with Robotic Specimen Handling

**BEAR (2020) and MAMA BEAR / expanded campaign (2024)** are the most extensively documented systems. BEAR demonstrated fully autonomous closed-loop operation: Bayesian optimization selected a structure design, OpenSCAD generated the STL, Slic3r produced G-code, OctoPrint managed the printer, the UR5e retrieved the part, weighed it, loaded it into the Instron 5965, and the compression test result fed back into Gaussian-process regression to guide the next experiment (gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 5-6). In the original campaign, 600 designs were tested in triplicate without human intervention; 32 experiments in 12 hours matched a 1,800-experiment grid campaign, and 64 experiments in 24 hours exceeded it (gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 4-5). The expanded campaign reported 25,387 experiments across seven materials (TPE, TPU-1/NinjaFlex, TPU-2/Cheetah, TPU-3/Armadillo, Nylon, PETG, PLA), with experiments running approximately 60% of wall-clock time and each mechanical test taking approximately 10 minutes (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 28-33, snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 2-3, snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 7-8). This directly contradicts any claim that no publication shows an arm unloading 3D printers inside a closed experimental loop. Human interventions included periodic manual bed cleaning when automated scraping failed after ten attempts, filament replacement, and polyimide tape maintenance (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 28-33). The authors state limitations including manufacturing variability (mass CV 4.6%, toughness CV 12.8%) and the need for human monitoring to modify campaign parameters during the multi-year operation (gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 2-3, snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 33-39).

**SmartLab (2025)** demonstrated a closed loop for tensile testing of ASTM D638 Type I specimens, varying raster angle and line distance across 90 specimens manufactured and tested without human specimen handling. The per-specimen handling cycle was 17 minutes (versus 9 minutes for a human researcher), but 24-hour continuous operation yielded a projected throughput of 21.1 specimens/day and 633/month versus 8.42/day and 252.6/month for human researchers working 8-hour shifts (yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 10-12, yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 12-13). The robotic researcher positioned specimens on the UTM with average errors of 268 μm and 0.19°, compared to 0.74° angular error for human researchers (yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 8-9). The main limitation was battery life (eight experimental cycles before manual recharging) and scheduling of multiple parallel tasks (yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 10-12, yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 13-13).

**Perception-driven polymer laboratory (Hernández-del-Valle et al. 2026, ChemRxiv preprint, DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv.15007960/v1).** This non-peer-reviewed preprint describes a TurtleBot 4 mobile robot with a UR10 cobot workcell processing injection-molded Charpy specimens (not FFF-printed). It processed 190 specimens in 274 minutes (1 min 26 s average per specimen), with a recoverable-error rate of 1.05% (one grasp failure and one incomplete cut detected and corrected) and two additional undetected incomplete cuts (1.05%) (hernandezdelvalle2026perceptiondrivenexperimentalworkflows pages 10-12). Telegram-based alerts and event-driven recovery reduced supervision to brief, occasional interventions, supporting a one-researcher-per-laboratory model rather than one-operator-per-instrument (hernandezdelvalle2026perceptiondrivenexperimentalworkflows pages 10-12, hernandezdelvalle2026perceptiondrivenexperimentalworkflows pages 12-14).

### (3) Camera-Based Print Monitoring and Verification

The following table summarizes reported accuracies for defect detection with camera-based systems:

| Reference / year | Method / architecture | Defect types detected | Camera type | Reported accuracy / metric | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Marin & Marin, 2024 | Modified DeepLabV3 semantic segmentation with Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling | Spaghetti / thin irregular filament | Webcam imagery | **95% accuracy** at dilation rate 18; 76%, 92%, and 88% at rates 6, 12, and 24 | Peer-reviewed journal article; performance may depend on lighting, image quality, and geometry. (marin20243dprintingerrors pages 2-4, marin20243dprintingerrors pages 1-2) |
| Aktepe & Ergün, 2026 | Transfer learning with EfficientNetB0 and MobileNetV2 | Cracking, layer shift, off-platform/detachment, stringing, and warping | Fixed monocular camera; no additional sensors | **87.7% overall accuracy** for EfficientNetB0; **97%** for MobileNetV2 | Peer-reviewed journal article; 1,912-image dataset. Confusion was reported particularly between cracking and layer shifting. (aktepe2026deeplearningapplication pages 3-6) |
| Lee et al., 2026 | ResNet-18 CNN monitoring extrusion at the nozzle | Low-flow-rate error and associated under-extrusion | Global-shutter camera | **96.1% overall classification accuracy** | Peer-reviewed conference-series article; global shutter reduced motion blur during high-speed printing. Evaluated extrusion-flow error rather than whole-part detachment or spaghetti. |
| Eisenhour / DaR3D, 2022 | Background removal and normalized mean-square image comparison | Print slippage / displacement from expected position | Periodically sampled low-cost webcam with controlled lighting | **89.6% accuracy** for identifying slippage | Thesis or other non-peer-reviewed academic source; evaluated samples from two printers. Camera placement, lighting, and background control affect transferability. (eisenhour2022thedar3dsystema pages 46-51) |
| Obico / The Spaghetti Detective | YOLOv2-based cloud inference on printer video | Primarily spaghetti; commercial monitoring may alert or stop a print | User-supplied webcam / livestream | **No independently validated accuracy or trial count located** | Commercial/open-source service rather than a peer-reviewed validation study. Published comparisons report weaker generalization when test imagery differs from training data. (charia2025realtimestringingdetection pages 2-4, eisenhour2022thedar3dsystema pages 46-51, marin20243dprintingerrors pages 1-2) |
| Islam et al., 2026 | Vision Transformer with global self-attention and depth-map surface representation | Normal surface, under-extrusion, over-extrusion, and void/empty regions | 2D laser-scanning-derived depth maps rather than an ordinary RGB webcam | **Macro-F1 0.877; macro mean AUC 0.972; 14.80–32.45 ms inference per patch** | Peer-reviewed journal article; supports real-time layer-wise inspection but is not a Raspberry-Pi-webcam-only implementation. |
| BEAR / MAMA BEAR, 2023–2024 | Arm-mounted camera verifies bed state; image check follows robotic scraper cleaning | Uncleared build plate / residual printed material before the next job | Camera mounted on UR5e robot arm | **No published classification accuracy, false-clear rate, or trial count** | Peer-reviewed 2024 system paper with detailed procedures in its earlier preprint. The robot makes up to ten scraper-cleaning attempts; persistent contamination disables that printer and alerts an operator. (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 28-33) |


*Table: Reported vision-system performance for common FFF failures and plate-clear verification. The table distinguishes peer-reviewed accuracy measurements from commercial claims and systems for which no validation rate was published.*

Key findings: Spaghetti/stringing detection using DeepLabV3 with tailored ASPP modules reached 95% accuracy at optimal dilation rate (marin20243dprintingerrors pages 2-4). Multi-class defect classification (cracking, layer shift, off-platform, stringing, warping) with MobileNetV2 transfer learning achieved 97% overall accuracy, while EfficientNetB0 reached 87.7%, with confusion primarily between cracking and layer shifting (aktepe2026deeplearningapplication pages 3-6). Extrusion flow-rate error detection using ResNet-18 with a global-shutter camera achieved 96.1% classification accuracy at both low and high print speeds. The DaR3D thesis system detected print slippage at 89.6% accuracy using webcam images with controlled lighting. The commercial Obico/Spaghetti Detective system uses YOLOv2 but no independently validated accuracy metric was located in peer-reviewed literature (charia2025realtimestringingdetection pages 2-4, eisenhour2022thedar3dsystema pages 46-51, marin20243dprintingerrors pages 1-2).

For **plate-clear verification**, the BEAR system uses an arm-mounted camera to check whether the bed is clear before each print, followed by robotic scraper cleaning with photographic verification after each attempt, up to ten retries (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 28-33). No published false-clear rate or classification accuracy for this verification step was found.

**No peer-reviewed study was found that specifically addresses automatic dimensional measurement of printed specimens before testing using low-cost cameras**, although SmartLab uses a wrist camera for dimension measurement with a reported 268 μm positional accuracy at the UTM (yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 8-9), and the perception-driven polymer lab uses YOLOv11 segmentation and ArUco-based pose estimation for specimen localization (hernandezdelvalle2026perceptiondrivenexperimentalworkflows pages 10-12, hernandezdelvalle2026perceptiondrivenexperimentalworkflows pages 4-5).

### (4) Print Farms with Robotic Tending

**No peer-reviewed publication was found that reports quantitative throughput, uptime, human-hours-per-print, or cost-per-part for a robotically tended FFF print farm in comparison to a manual farm.** The FlexTrak thesis describes a modular system designed to attach one removal mechanism per printer, enabling queued production through OctoPrint on Raspberry Pis, with the goal of continuous operation requiring human intervention only for filament spool replacement every few days (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 1-7, me2020increasing3dprinter pages 7-9). However, the planned reliability tests (overnight, weekend, and full-spool runs) were proposed rather than reported (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 7-9). Budzik et al. (2024) describe a conceptual robotic MEX cell in which a collaborative arm transfers platforms and parts but provide no measured farm-level metrics (budzik2024possibilitiesofautomating pages 3-5, budzik2024possibilitiesofautomating pages 1-2). Post-processing is estimated to add approximately 17–100% to printing time and roughly 30% of manufacturing cost, with labor costs of approximately USD 30–100/hour (dizon2021postprocessingof3dprinted pages 28-29). These figures suggest substantial economic incentive for automation but remain indirect comparisons rather than controlled farm studies. **This represents a clear gap in the published literature.**

### (5) Remote or Cloud Users Submitting Design-Print-Test Jobs

**SmartLab Tanzania pilot (2025):** Twenty-one students at Arusha Technical College in Tanzania remotely conducted material-testing experiments on equipment hosted at Seoul National University in Korea. Students controlled the system via a GUI and monitored it through real-time 360° VR streaming; temporary network disconnections did not halt experiments, as recorded VR video could be replayed (yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 10-12, yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 9-10). Two full cycles of material testing were successfully completed remotely (yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 9-10). The system tolerated unstable network conditions without significant interruption to experimental procedures (yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 10-12, yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 13-13). No numerical job-completion rate or turnaround-time distribution was reported.

**BEAR external-user pilot:** No measured outcomes (completion rate, turnaround, interventions) for external users submitting jobs to the BEAR system were found in the accessible published literature. The BEAR data are reportedly available through kablab.org/data (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 33-39), but no publication describing external-user pilot results was located.

**No other published cloud-lab design-print-test system with measured user outcomes was identified.** This area remains largely undocumented in the peer-reviewed literature.

### (6) Feasibility Analysis for the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab

**Adhesion forces.** Kaščak et al. (2024, *Applied Sciences*, DOI: 10.3390/app14020945) measured PETG tear-off force on a PEI-coated spring-steel build plate at 53.48 ± 7.95 N (mean ± SD over 12 trials), compared with 33.09 ± 5.52 N on uncoated aluminum (kascak2024adhesiontestingdevice pages 8-9). PLA was explicitly excluded from that study because it "generally adheres sufficiently to commonly used uncontaminated surfaces" (kascak2024adhesiontestingdevice pages 6-8). **No peer-reviewed measurement of PLA adhesion force on textured PEI was located**, representing a data gap. Higher bed temperature generally increases adhesion, with temperatures slightly above the glass-transition temperature recommended for first-layer bonding (kascak2024adhesiontestingdevice pages 2-4). PETG showed higher shear resistance than PLA on aluminum substrates: 5.94 MPa vs. 3.92 MPa at their respective optimal conditions (camposjurado2025manufacturingofpolymer–metal pages 12-14).

**Sheet-flexing forces.** The FlexTrak system measured approximately 15.48 N normal force to break Prusa MK3 magnetic bed retention and 6.76 N horizontal pull after the edge was lifted (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 60-70, me2020increasing3dprinter pages 56-60). This is well within the PiPER arm's 15 N gripper force specification, but the arm's J5 ±70° wrist limitation would make straight-down grasps near the table infeasible. Sheet flexing was rated the most reliable removal method, requiring the least effort and posing minimal risk of part damage in a qualitative evaluation (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 19-23, me2020increasing3dprinter pages 37-42).

**Feasibility for the PiPER arm on A1 mini bed-slingers.** The A1 mini is a bed-slinger (Y-axis moves the bed), which means the magnetic spring-steel sheet can in principle be slid off the bed by the arm. With approximately 15 N of gripping force, the PiPER could grip the sheet edge and pull it, since horizontal pull requires only about 6.76 N (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 60-70). However, the 53 N tear-off force for PETG on PEI significantly exceeds the arm's force budget, so direct scraping or perpendicular prying of well-adhered parts would likely fail. The recommended strategy for small PLA toys is: (a) allow cooling to room temperature (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 23-26), which substantially reduces adhesion on textured PEI; (b) slide the magnetic sheet off the bed (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 60-70); and (c) flex the sheet to pop parts free, as commercial flex plates "require the least effort" and are "reliable" with "minimal risk of part damage" (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 19-23). The ±70° J5 limitation means the arm should approach the bed edge laterally rather than from directly above.

**Grasping irregular printed parts.** No study specifically examining parallel-gripper grasping of irregular 3D-printed parts was found. General robotic grasping literature reports that underactuated grippers achieve 90–98% success rates on mixed-object benchmarks, and CNN-based grasp planners on parallel grippers can handle unknown objects including those with irregular shapes. For the specific case of small printed toys, compliant or soft-padded parallel jaw inserts would improve grasp stability. PETG inserts with 30% hexagonal infill showed distinct friction and wear behavior compared to bulk polymers, suggesting that printed gripper jaw liners could be customized for the application. The 1.5 kg payload of the PiPER arm is well above the mass of small PLA toys (typically <50 g) but would limit handling of multiple parts simultaneously or large fixtures.

**Practical recommendations for the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab:** (1) For the December A1 mini toy batch, flexing the magnetic PEI sheet after cooling to room temperature is the most feasible and best-documented approach within the arm's force budget. (2) For later mechanical testing (tensegrity compression/drop tests), the BEAR paradigm of robot-arm transfer between printer, scale, and testing machine is directly applicable and proven at >25,000-experiment scale. (3) Camera-based bed-clear verification should be implemented following the BEAR protocol (arm-mounted camera check with retry logic), and spaghetti/failure detection using MobileNetV2 or similar lightweight models can achieve ≥95% accuracy with modest training data. (4) The main gap for the BYU setup is the absence of published PLA-on-textured-PEI adhesion force data and the lack of demonstrated autonomous sheet-flex removal on bed-slinger printers specifically, both of which would benefit from in-house characterization experiments.

After printing, the bed is heated for TPE and TPU-1/2 (100 °C) to facilitate removal, or allowed to cool to 30 °C for PLA, PETG, Nylon, and TPU-3 (pqac-00000041). Failure modes include dirty beds, unsuccessful component grabs, misorientation, mass/height deviations >5%, severe print defects, insufficient strain data, and periodic need to replace worn polyimide tape and load new filament rolls (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000038). No explicit handling success-rate percentage was reported.

**FlexTrak automated sheet-flexing system (thesis, 2020).** This non-peer-reviewed student project describes a modular system for the Prusa i3 MK3 that elevates the magnetic spring-steel sheet off the bed (requiring approximately 15.48 N normal force to break magnetic retention, and 6.76 N horizontal pull), feeds it through a curved bending track using powered rollers, and uses passive scrapers to remove remaining debris (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). A decision-matrix comparison rated sheet flexing higher than disposable roll media (3.75 vs. 3.1) for reliability, modularity, and maintainability (pqac-00000018). Scraper-only removal was tested and found unreliable: it damaged small parts, retained parts on the blade, was limited to about 38% of the bed area (150 cm² maximum on a 400 cm² bed), required favorable part orientation and rafts, and produced visible scrape marks after 250 cycles (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000022). Print-head collision/ejection was also described, wherein modified G-code causes the print head to ram the part off; this requires no hardware modification but needs parts approximately 1 inch tall and becomes harder as contact area increases (pqac-00000017). Overnight, weekend, and full-spool reliability tests were planned but not quantitatively reported (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000061).

### (2) Closed-Loop Design-Print-Test Systems with Robotic Specimen Handling

**BEAR (2020) and MAMA BEAR / expanded campaign (2024)** are the most extensively documented systems. BEAR demonstrated fully autonomous closed-loop operation: Bayesian optimization selected a structure design, OpenSCAD generated the STL, Slic3r produced G-code, OctoPrint managed the printer, the UR5e retrieved the part, weighed it, loaded it into the Instron 5965, and the compression test result fed back into Gaussian-process regression to guide the next experiment (pqac-00000004). In the original campaign, 600 designs were tested in triplicate without human intervention; 32 experiments in 12 hours matched a 1,800-experiment grid campaign, and 64 experiments in 24 hours exceeded it (pqac-00000006). The expanded campaign reported 25,387 experiments across seven materials (TPE, TPU-1/NinjaFlex, TPU-2/Cheetah, TPU-3/Armadillo, Nylon, PETG, PLA), with experiments running approximately 60% of wall-clock time and each mechanical test taking approximately 10 minutes (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000039). This directly contradicts any claim that no publication shows an arm unloading 3D printers inside a closed experimental loop. Human interventions included periodic manual bed cleaning when automated scraping failed after ten attempts, filament replacement, and polyimide tape maintenance (pqac-00000038). The authors state limitations including manufacturing variability (mass CV 4.6%, toughness CV 12.8%) and the need for human monitoring to modify campaign parameters during the multi-year operation (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000040).

**SmartLab (2025)** demonstrated a closed loop for tensile testing of ASTM D638 Type I specimens, varying raster angle and line distance across 90 specimens manufactured and tested without human specimen handling. The per-specimen handling cycle was 17 minutes (versus 9 minutes for a human researcher), but 24-hour continuous operation yielded a projected throughput of 21.1 specimens/day and 633/month versus 8.42/day and 252.6/month for human researchers working 8-hour shifts (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000010). The robotic researcher positioned specimens on the UTM with average errors of 268 μm and 0.19°, compared to 0.74° angular error for human researchers (pqac-00000011). The main limitation was battery life (eight experimental cycles before manual recharging) and scheduling of multiple parallel tasks (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009).

**Perception-driven polymer laboratory (Hernández-del-Valle et al. 2026, ChemRxiv preprint, DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv.15007960/v1).** This non-peer-reviewed preprint describes a TurtleBot 4 mobile robot with a UR10 cobot workcell processing injection-molded Charpy specimens (not FFF-printed). It processed 190 specimens in 274 minutes (1 min 26 s average per specimen), with a recoverable-error rate of 1.05% (one grasp failure and one incomplete cut detected and corrected) and two additional undetected incomplete cuts (1.05%) (pqac-00000050). Telegram-based alerts and event-driven recovery reduced supervision to brief, occasional interventions, supporting a one-researcher-per-laboratory model rather than one-operator-per-instrument (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000056).

These figures suggest substantial economic incentive for automation but remain indirect comparisons rather than controlled farm studies. **This represents a clear gap in the published literature.**

### (5) Remote or Cloud Users Submitting Design-Print-Test Jobs

**SmartLab Tanzania pilot (2025):** Twenty-one students at Arusha Technical College in Tanzania remotely conducted material-testing experiments on equipment hosted at Seoul National University in Korea. Students controlled the system via a GUI and monitored it through real-time 360° VR streaming; temporary network disconnections did not halt experiments, as recorded VR video could be replayed (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000068). Two full cycles of material testing were successfully completed remotely (pqac-00000068). The system tolerated unstable network conditions without significant interruption to experimental procedures (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000067). No numerical job-completion rate or turnaround-time distribution was reported.

**BEAR external-user pilot:** No measured outcomes (completion rate, turnaround, interventions) for external users submitting jobs to the BEAR system were found in the accessible published literature. The BEAR data are reportedly available through kablab.org/data (pqac-00000040), but no publication describing external-user pilot results was located.

**No other published cloud-lab design-print-test system with measured user outcomes was identified.** This area remains largely undocumented in the peer-reviewed literature.

### (6) Feasibility Analysis for the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab

**Adhesion forces.** Kaščak et al. (2024, *Applied Sciences*, DOI: 10.3390/app14020945) measured PETG tear-off force on a PEI-coated spring-steel build plate at 53.48 ± 7.95 N (mean ± SD over 12 trials), compared with 33.09 ± 5.52 N on uncoated aluminum (pqac-00000025). PLA was explicitly excluded from that study because it "generally adheres sufficiently to commonly used uncontaminated surfaces" (pqac-00000024). **No peer-reviewed measurement of PLA adhesion force on textured PEI was located**, representing a data gap. Higher bed temperature generally increases adhesion, with temperatures slightly above the glass-transition temperature recommended for first-layer bonding (pqac-00000026). PETG showed higher shear resistance than PLA on aluminum substrates: 5.94 MPa vs. 3.92 MPa at their respective optimal conditions (pqac-00000029).

**Sheet-flexing forces.** The FlexTrak system measured approximately 15.48 N normal force to break Prusa MK3 magnetic bed retention and 6.76 N horizontal pull after the edge was lifted (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). This is well within the PiPER arm's 15 N gripper force specification, but the arm's J5 ±70° wrist limitation would make straight-down grasps near the table infeasible. Sheet flexing was rated the most reliable removal method, requiring the least effort and posing minimal risk of part damage in a qualitative evaluation (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020).

**Feasibility for the PiPER arm on A1 mini bed-slingers.** The A1 mini is a bed-slinger (Y-axis moves the bed), which means the magnetic spring-steel sheet can in principle be slid off the bed by the arm. With approximately 15 N of gripping force, the PiPER could grip the sheet edge and pull it, since horizontal pull requires only about 6.76 N (pqac-00000015). However, the 53 N tear-off force for PETG on PEI significantly exceeds the arm's force budget, so direct scraping or perpendicular prying of well-adhered parts would likely fail. The recommended strategy for small PLA toys is: (a) allow cooling to room temperature (the BEAR system uses 30 °C for PLA removal; pqac-00000041), which substantially reduces adhesion on textured PEI; (b) slide the magnetic sheet off the bed (requiring <16 N; pqac-00000015); and (c) flex the sheet to pop parts free, as commercial flex plates "require the least effort" and are "reliable" with "minimal risk of part damage" (pqac-00000019). The ±70° J5 limitation means the arm should approach the bed edge laterally rather than from directly above.

**Grasping irregular printed parts.** No study specifically examining parallel-gripper grasping of irregular 3D-printed parts was found. General robotic grasping literature reports that underactuated grippers achieve 90–98% success rates on mixed-object benchmarks, and CNN-based grasp planners on parallel grippers can handle unknown objects including those with irregular shapes. For the specific case of small printed toys, compliant or soft-padded parallel jaw inserts would improve grasp stability. PETG inserts with 30% hexagonal infill showed distinct friction and wear behavior compared to bulk polymers, suggesting that printed gripper jaw liners could be customized for the application. The 1.5 kg payload of the PiPER arm is well above the mass of small PLA toys (typically <50 g) but would limit handling of multiple parts simultaneously or large fixtures.

**Practical recommendations for the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab:** (1) For the December A1 mini toy batch, flexing the magnetic PEI sheet after cooling to room temperature is the most feasible and best-documented approach within the arm's force budget. (2) For later mechanical testing (tensegrity compression/drop tests), the BEAR paradigm of robot-arm transfer between printer, scale, and testing machine is directly applicable and proven at >25,000-experiment scale. (3) Camera-based bed-clear verification should be implemented following the BEAR protocol (arm-mounted camera check with retry logic), and spaghetti/failure detection using MobileNetV2 or similar lightweight models can achieve ≥95% accuracy with modest training data. (4) The main gap for the BYU setup is the absence of published PLA-on-textured-PEI adhesion force data and the lack of demonstrated autonomous sheet-flex removal on bed-slinger printers specifically, both of which would benefit from in-house characterization experiments.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes BEAR as an autonomous, centrally controlled experimental platform for discovering high-performing 3D-printed structures. Its hardware includes five fused-filament-fabrication 3D printers, a scale, a universal testing machine, and a six-axis robotic arm that transfers experiments among stations. A custom MATLAB script controls the system, which performs user-prioritized tasks without direct human intervention. Experiment selection uses Bayesian optimization: surrogate models predict peak energy-absorbing efficiency (Ks*), threshold stress, and printability from an input space comprising 11 geometric parameters and two material properties. Gaussian-process regressions model Ks* and threshold stress, while a one-hidden-layer neural network predicts whether a design-material combination can be printed. Acquisition policies include maximum variance, expected improvement, and upper confidence bound, with predicted printability used to favor realizable components and, in some policies, threshold-stress targets incorporated as an additional objective. contexts.context: The excerpt describes BEAR as an autonomous closed-loop system that converts a candidate crossed-barrel design, represented by parameters x = (n, θ, r, t), into an STL file with OpenSCAD, converts the STL to g-code with Slic3r, and sends the print job through OctoPrint. After printing and cooling, a robotic arm retrieves the structure, which is weighed and tested; measurements are stored in a local database. Gaussian-process regression (GPR) updates the system’s belief model, while a decision-making policy chooses the next design from randomly sampled candidates. A MATLAB script coordinates the equipment without a human in the loop. Mechanical evaluation consists of uniaxial compression at 3 mm/min up to a 4.8-kN force threshold, with toughness calculated as the area under the force–displacement curve. Curves are truncated when force falls below 50 N after the first 2 mm to exclude loading fragments of a fractured barrel. The reported efficiency benchmark is that, although more than 2,500 experiments were conducted across the work, only 32 experiments were needed to reach an optimal structure. This excerpt does not identify the robot-arm model, printer model(s), overall printing/test success rate, throughput in parts per unit time, or a complete taxonomy of failure modes; it only indicates fracture-related measurement handling.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that SmartLab, a mobile-manipulator-based remote laboratory located at Seoul National University, successfully supported remote 3D-printing material-testing education in Tanzania. Twenty-one students participated in the remote experiment, with one group controlling the system and another observing real-time broadcasts and 360° VR streaming. The system enabled GUI-based remote monitoring and control, live experimental data, camera views, task progress, and replay of recorded VR video when network disruptions affected real-time monitoring. Despite unstable network conditions and limited infrastructure, remote material testing proceeded without significant interruptions, indicating strong operational success, although no numerical success-rate percentage is provided. For automated specimen testing, SmartLab performed a full-factorial experiment on ASTM D638 Type 1 specimens, varying raster angle and line distance across 90 experiments, with no human specimen handling. Its average handling cycle was 17 minutes per specimen, slower than the 9-minute human-researcher cycle. However, automation increased theoretical throughput to 664 specimens per month versus 252 for human researchers. Human intervention was still needed to recharge the robotic researcher because its battery lasted eight experimental cycles and no automatic charging dock was available. Thus, the system demonstrated successful remote automation and higher potential throughput, with charging remaining a practical limitation.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports automation results for a distributed polymer laboratory using a TurtleBot 4 mobile robot and cobot workcells. The mobile robot completed 12 transport tasks, corresponding to approximately 96 trips over six hours, with a charging pause when battery charge fell below 30%. For specimen manipulation—specifically residual sprue cutting after injection molding—the system processed 190 specimens in 274 minutes (4 hours 34 minutes), averaging 1 minute 26 seconds per specimen. This is relevant to automated specimen testing workflows, although the excerpt describes injection-molded specimens rather than 3D-printed parts and does not provide a dedicated 3D-printing throughput figure. Two recoverable errors occurred, giving a 1.05% recoverable-error rate; two additional incomplete cuts were not detected, also representing 1.05% of specimens. The workflow included detection, grasp and cut verification, tray storage, and tray changes. It was not fully autonomous: material charging and changing still required human intervention, and some defects could require operator action. However, warnings via Telegram and event-driven recovery reduced supervision to brief, occasional interventions, supporting a human-in-the-loop model in which one researcher could manage the laboratory rather than one operator per instrument.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports SmartLab’s automated 3D-printing specimen experiment and compares its throughput with human researchers. Fabrication and tensile testing each took the same time in both workflows: 48 minutes for fabrication and 5 minutes for tensile testing. SmartLab required more time for dimension measurement (6 minutes versus 2) and navigation between equipment (6 minutes versus 2), resulting in 65 minutes per specimen compared with 57 minutes for human researchers. Despite the longer per-specimen cycle, SmartLab’s continuous 24-hour operation produced a substantially higher calculated throughput: 21.1 specimens per day versus 8.42 for humans working an 8-hour day, and 633 specimens per month versus 252.6. The article also describes an automatic experiment mode that generated averaged elastic-modulus results from 90 specimens. Regarding remote operation, the system was demonstrated between Seoul National University in Korea and ATC in Tanzania, showing that students could conduct real-time experiments using advanced laboratory equipment. The excerpt emphasizes flexible integration of legacy equipment, interoperable control, and a hierarchical architecture consisting of user-interface, experimentation, and equipment-integration layers. However, it does not provide a numerical automation success rate or quantify the frequency of human intervention during mobile-manipulator operation.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an automated build-plate removal system based on flexing/raising a magnetic removable bed, powered rollers, and passive scraping. Because the Prusa magnetic bed could not be pulled directly from the front, an elevator first breaks the magnetic retention and raises the bed 52 mm; rollers then feed it into a bending track. Measured force requirements were approximately 16 N normal to the bed to overcome magnetic retention (more precisely, 15.48 N in the later force analysis) and 6.76 N to pull the bed horizontally after its edge was lifted. The selected lead-screw stepper motors could provide 122 N and had a maximum torque of 0.04 N·m, versus a calculated initial lifting torque of 5.91 × 10^-3 N·m. The rollers were driven by a 52-rpm, 2 N·m gear motor; calculated required roller torque was 6.8 × 10^-2 N·m. Flexing breaks most part-to-bed adhesion, but residual material requires a passive scraper. The final scraper was shortened and chamfered for earlier engagement and consisted of nine components spanning the system width. This excerpt does not report success rate, cycle time, bed temperature for release, or alternative removal methods such as print-head ejection, conveyor-only removal, or tilting the bed.

contexts.context: The excerpt primarily evaluates an automated scraper and briefly describes print-head collision/ejection. Scraping failed on both a large block without a raft and a small 25 mm star; it also damaged the star’s leading point. The authors conclude that the tested scraper could not remove prints without rafts. Earlier testing suggested a maximum removable bottom area of 150 cm², while the printer bed was 400 cm², limiting usable area to 38%. Removal also depended on print orientation: corners or curved edges should face the scraper because edges parallel to it were difficult to remove. A 250-cycle scraper test produced substantial scrape marks on the simulated print surface, indicating bed-wear concerns. The excerpt does not provide quantified scraper forces, success percentages, or cycle times. The collision method modifies G-code so the print head rams the completed part off the bed; it requires no hardware modification but is unsuitable for very small or low-height parts, generally requiring about 1 inch of height, and becomes harder as the contact area increases. The bed remains hot during ejection because there is no cooling interval. No information is provided here about flexing sheets, tilting beds, conveyor belts, measured release temperatures, or comparative success rates and cycle times.

contexts.context: The excerpt compares automated removal approaches centered on a disposable conveyor/belt system and a flexing build plate. In the disposable design, a roll of material is placed behind the printer; a driven roller advances and clamps fresh material onto the bed, and after printing pulls the material forward while a linear blade cuts off the used section. This provides continuous preparation for the next print, but material testing identified adhesion and warping problems. Transparency produced the best surface finish and was relatively easy to remove, while cardboard and present paper adhered too strongly; aluminum foil produced warping and detached after multiple layers. The flexing-sheet concept prints on a reusable sheet-metal plate that is mechanically bent to release the part, similar to commercial flex beds. It was judged autonomous, minimally maintained, non-damaging, and more reliable because printing occurs on the stock printer surface. The decision matrix rated bed flex higher overall than disposable roll (3.75 versus 3.1), particularly for reliability, modularity, maintainability, size, and sensor capability. Scrapers are listed as a FlexTrak subsystem, but this excerpt gives no scraping results. It also provides no quantitative removal forces, success rates, cycle times, bed-release temperatures, tilting-bed method, or print-head-ejection method.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses manual removal methods relevant to automated build-plate release, especially scraping and flexing. Scraping can use a constant pushing force against the part edge or an impulse force delivered by striking the scraper with a heavy object such as a mallet. However, the excerpt does not quantify the required force, success rate, or cycle time; it only warns that excessive scraping can damage the bed and that sharp tools pose an injury risk. Removable flex plates can be bent repeatedly to break adhesion, allowing the part to pop off. They are characterized qualitatively as requiring the least effort, being reliable, and having minimal risk of part damage, but no numerical success rate or release force is provided. The excerpt also describes thermal shocking of removable beds: the bed is heated to 60°C and submerged in room-temperature water at 20°C. Unequal thermal contraction between the bed and plastic weakens adhesion, and release works best immediately after printing, before the bed and part have fully cooled. No information is provided here on tilting beds, conveyor belts, print-head ejection, or comparative automated cycle times.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an automated removal approach called “FlexTrak,” combining bed removal, sheet flexing, and scraping. The print bed is first removed from the printer and fed through a bearing-based bending track. The track bends the sheet over a 50 mm vertical displacement across 270 mm, using powered rollers or wheels; this flexing is intended to break adhesion between the printed part and the bed. Scrapers then remove residual adhesion and small plastic fragments that remain after flexing. For the Prusa i3 Mk3 implementation, rubber wheels were selected instead of sprockets to drive the original magnetic bed, with the wheels transmitting 2 Nm of torque. Because the magnetic bed could not simply be pulled forward, an elevator mechanism was added to break the magnetic hold before horizontal transport. Measured forces were 16 N normal to the bed to overcome magnetic retention and 6.76 N horizontally after the bed edge had been lifted. The excerpt does not report a quantitative removal success rate, cycle time, bed temperature required for release, or comparative results for tilting-bed, conveyor-belt, or print-head-ejection methods. It therefore provides mechanical design and force data rather than a full performance comparison.

contexts.context: The excerpt compares several build-plate and automated-removal approaches. A scraper is considered feasible on a rigid glass plate, but the reviewed mechanized scraper had important limitations: parts had to use a raft, remain below 150 cm², and be oriented with a corner toward the scraper. It did not detect print completion automatically, so users had to enter an estimated print time, and it transported parts unreliably—large parts could fall off the bed while small parts could remain on the scraper. Flexible sheets offer a gentler removal method. Easy-Peelzy uses a magnetic underside and can be bent to peel the print away gradually; the authors describe this as easier than scraping or pulling directly and identify its ability to bend around a radius as promising for a passive conveyor-belt design. BuildTak FlexPlate works similarly but lacks magnetic backing, requiring a separate clamping mechanism and allowing use with magnetic or nonmagnetic beds. The excerpt also notes that filament properties affect removal: PLA is brittle and requires consideration to avoid damage, while ABS, PETG, and TPU are described as ductile. No quantitative removal forces, success rates, cycle times, tilting-bed or print-head-ejection results, or measured bed temperature required for release are provided here.

contexts.context: The excerpt primarily evaluates a scraper-based automated part-removal design. Successful removal was defined by completely breaking adhesion between the print and bed and completely clearing the print from the bed and print area. In one test, scraping a 3-inch PLA cylinder with a raft took approximately one minute. The blade could slide beneath the part and break adhesion, but the part often remained on top of the scraper rather than being discharged. This was considered a failure because the scraper would need to re-enter the print area and the retained part could fall back onto the bed and interfere with subsequent jobs. Multiple-part removal was also unsuccessful: one part did not fully clear the bed and two remained on the scraper. A larger 5-inch cylinder fell off the side of the bed, technically satisfying removal criteria but demonstrating inconsistent discharge behavior. The scraper also visibly deflected before breaking adhesion, indicating insufficient removal force and mechanical strain on the arm and lead screws. The prior system’s stated design goals were sufficient force and accurate, repeatable motion, but removed-part destinations varied with part size. The excerpt does not provide quantified force measurements, overall success-rate percentages, bed-release temperatures, or comparisons with flexing sheets, tilting beds, conveyor belts, or print-head ejection. It notes that testing used rafts, approximately 3 mm thick, which make scraping easier but require later manual removal.

contexts.context: The excerpt surveys automated 3D-print removal methods, with the most detailed discussion covering scraping and conveyor belts. In the NVBots scraper system, a blade travels across the build bed, pushes the completed part against a wall, and then reverses to move the part into a collection bin. The method can handle different print sizes and large bed coverage, but it depends on highly consistent bed leveling and bed height so the blade contacts the interface between part and bed rather than the part itself. Excessive removal resistance produces high lead-screw torque and may damage the mechanism. The integrated design is difficult to adapt modularly and cannot readily be combined with other removal methods. Conveyor-belt printers remove parts by rolling the belt forward; rigid prints peel away from the belt at the roller. This approach supports consecutive printing and potentially unlimited print length, with one described system advancing approximately one belt rotation before starting the next print. The excerpt also mentions disposable sheets and other approaches, but it does not provide quantitative removal forces, success rates, cycle times, or bed temperatures for release. It likewise does not specifically describe flexing-sheet, tilting-bed, or print-head-ejection implementations beyond noting that multiple methods have tradeoffs.

contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant to measuring the force required to detach an FFF-printed part and to understanding temperature effects on first-layer adhesion, but it does not provide specific adhesion-force values for PLA or PETG on PEI or textured PEI sheets. It describes the broader purpose of the authors’ device: measuring adhesion across different print-bed materials and adapting the design to various FFF printer constructions. The literature review identifies several measurement approaches. Perpendicular tensile testing measures force normal to the print bed and is presented as suitable for evaluating initial-layer adhesion, while shear-off testing measures force parallel to the printed layers. Prior work found that print-bed temperature significantly affects adhesion, with higher temperatures improving adhesion; a bed heated slightly above the filament’s glass-transition temperature was recommended. The excerpt also notes studies using PLA on textile substrates, PLA and ABS on multiple bed types, and borosilicate glass or polyamide surfaces. These findings support examining temperature and surface texture when comparing PEI substrates, but the supplied pages do not report PETG results, PEI-specific measurements, textured-sheet comparisons, or numerical detachment forces.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general principles relevant to measuring adhesion between 3D-printed plastics and a build plate, but it does not report specific adhesion-force values for PLA or PETG on smooth PEI, textured PEI, or any required detachment force. It explains that adhesion depends on the bulk materials and the interfacial zone, and may arise from van der Waals forces, chemical bonding, or electrostatic attraction. Surface energy and wettability are emphasized: metals generally have higher surface energy than polymers, while increased temperature can raise internal energy and make the surfaces wet each other more readily. The text also notes that solid-to-solid wetting is especially relevant because deposited plastic is molten or semi-solid during printing and then rapidly cools and hardens. Relative surface energy is proposed to be estimated indirectly through water interactions, using hydrophobicity and hydrophilicity. PLA and PETG are identified among the commonly used thermoplastics tested in the broader study, but this passage does not compare their adhesion on PEI surfaces, distinguish smooth from textured PEI sheets, describe a force-detachment test, or quantify temperature-dependent adhesion. Thus, it supports the conceptual role of temperature, surface energy, and wetting, rather than the requested measurement results or experimental protocol.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides comparative adhesion data for PLA and PETG printed onto aluminum, rather than onto a PEI build plate or textured PEI sheet. It measures lap-shear adhesion strength, not the direct force required to detach a printed part from a build plate. Nevertheless, it indicates a clear temperature effect in combination with substrate preparation. For PLA on acid-etched aluminum, the maximum reported shear strength was 3.92 MPa at a 65 °C bed temperature; abrasive blasting at 65 °C reached 3.07 MPa. Higher bed temperature or less aggressive preparation reduced adhesion, with fine sanding at 85 °C producing only 0.52 MPa. For PETG, acid etching produced 5.94 MPa at 90 °C and 4.45 MPa at 110 °C, while abrasive blasting at 90 °C reached 4.89 MPa. Thus, PETG showed higher shear resistance than PLA under the tested aluminum conditions. The excerpt also reports bending-delamination results: PLA with abrasive or acid treatment at 65 °C had 50% success, whereas PETG with abrasive treatment at 90 °C had 62.5% and acid treatment at 90 °C only 12.5%. These results should not be directly generalized to PEI surfaces because material, texture, test geometry, and failure mode differ.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that the BEAR experimental campaign conducted 25,387 experiments. Materials explicitly mentioned in the procedures include TPE, TPU-1-2, PLA, PETG, Nylon, and TPU-3; Figure S4 is referenced for the material designations, but the complete material list is not provided here. For component removal, the printer bed was heated for TPE and TPU-1-2, while it was allowed to cool for PLA, PETG, Nylon, and TPU-3. The robot arm then removed the component and transferred it to a scale for mass measurement. Before each print, an arm-mounted camera checked whether the bed was clear. If cleaning was required, the robot arm used a scraper, repeating the cleaning attempt up to ten times and taking a verification photograph afterward. If the bed remained dirty, the printer was deactivated and an operator was notified to clean it manually. The excerpt does not provide the campaign’s throughput per day or system uptime. It indicates that human intervention was needed for persistent bed contamination, as well as periodic manual replacement of worn or damaged polyimide tape and loading new filament rolls.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes review and additional testing of a previous automated print-removal system, rather than the complete MAMA BEAR system. The documented tests included a 3-inch PLA cylinder with a standard raft, a multiple-part test involving three parts, and a 5-inch-diameter cylinder. The removal mechanism was a scraper blade that slid beneath the printed part to break adhesion and push it away from the print bed. Results were inconsistent: smaller parts commonly remained stuck on the scraper, while one large circular print fell off the side of the bed. The scraper also deflected before breaking adhesion, indicating insufficient removal force and mechanical strain. The previous team had tested only prints with rafts; the new team planned additional testing of prints without rafts, noting that rafts make blade insertion easier but require later manual removal. It does provide related information about a six-axis robotic-arm pellet-extrusion system. Materials identified as suitable for direct extrusion include recycled polypropylene (PP), wood–plastic composites (WPC), and carbon- or glass-fiber-reinforced polyamide (CF/GF-reinforced PA). Pellet feeding reportedly increases deposition speed by 5–8 times relative to filament extrusion. The developed end-effector is described as achieving an extrusion flow rate of 25 kg per hour, although another section specifies an adjustable throughput of 0–18 kg per hour for the particular screw/servomotor configuration; neither figure is converted into daily production. Cooling is provided by an annular air shroud using compressed air: four slit outlets direct co-flowing air at a 20-degree angle, cooling the deposited layer below its glass-transition temperature in less than 60 milliseconds. The robot arm is characterized by six-axis path flexibility, including non-coplanar deposition and overhangs, but no scraper mechanism is mentioned.

This setup enables high-throughput fabrication, ejection, and testing of many coupons without transferring them to an independent testing platform. contexts.context: ATCAM ejects each printed dynamic coupon using an in situ actuator (ISA) integrated into the printer setup. The coupon is designed as a sphere with a specially shaped base that provides a reliable deployment surface. The base includes a cavity that reduces the area contacting the build plate and therefore lowers the force needed for ejection. After deployment, the actuator sends the coupon along a trajectory toward an acrylic target attached to the load cell, where its impact is measured. The system is then able to reuse the cleared build surface to print and eject the next coupon. The actuator is described as generating 2 N of force, and the coupon geometry was selected for reliable deployment within that force limit. The excerpt states that the ejection/deployment process was repeated 100 times per ISA before manual removal, which was identified as the experimentally determined nondestructive lifespan of the actuator. However, the excerpt does not report a numerical ejection success rate or percentage. It only indicates that the geometry and setup were intended to make deployment reliable and repeatable; the requirement for at least 1 N of sensed impact force was a data-logging threshold, not an explicit ejection-success criterion.

The blade moves underneath a completed part to break adhesion with the print bed, then is intended to push or carry the part out of the print area. The only described part that fell away was a large 5-inch cylinder, which tipped off the side of the bed; this behavior was considered inconsistent. Thus, the excerpt supports identifying the mechanism as scraper-based mechanical ejection, but it does not establish a quantitative success rate for coupon ejection. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a perception-driven polymer laboratory integrating a TurtleBot 4 mobile robot with cobot-based specimen manipulation and injection-molding workflows. The mobile robot performed repeated transport tasks between workcells, completing 12 tasks or approximately 96 trips over six hours, with a charging pause when battery level fell below 30%. The specimen-handling workflow processed 190 injection-molded specimens in 274 minutes (4 hours 34 minutes), corresponding to an average throughput of one specimen every 1 minute 26 seconds. The workflow included specimen detection, grasping, grasp verification, alignment, sprue cutting, cut verification, storage, and tray changes. Two recoverable errors occurred: one grasping failure and one incomplete cut, for a recoverable-error rate of 1.05%; verification steps enabled correction. Two additional incomplete-cut errors were not detected, also representing 1.05%, and could require later rejection or human correction. The system uses ArUco fiducial markers, YOLOv11 specimen segmentation, camera-readable trays, and ROS 2 navigation. It supports human-in-the-loop operation rather than fully autonomous continuous operation because injection molding still requires interventions such as material charging and replacement. The excerpt does not provide information about 3D printing or a general overall success rate beyond these task and error statistics.

The system integrates a 3D printer, dimensional measurement tools, a digital scale, and a universal testing machine (UTM). contexts.context: The excerpt provides a qualitative comparison between manual and automated 3D-print-farm operation, but it does not report numerical throughput, uptime, human-hours-per-print, labor cost, or cost-per-part measurements. In the manual workflow, an operator must remove each completed print and start the next job; this creates downtime and makes printer throughput dependent on operator availability and performance. The proposed automated system uses a print queue in OctoPrint on a Raspberry Pi. After a print finishes, it removes the part by flexing a removable bed through a curved track, returns the bed to the printer, and starts the next queued job. For printers without removable beds, a clamping mechanism and custom removable bed are used. The intended benefits are continuous operation, reduced cycle-to-cycle downtime, reduced direct human involvement, and the ability to manage multiple jobs in succession. Testing showed successful full removal cycles without human interaction, while longer-duration overnight, weekend, and full-filament-spool tests were identified as future reliability tests rather than reported results. The system is designed to be modular and scalable across multiple printers. Therefore, the excerpt supports the expectation of improved uptime and lower operator hours per print compared with manual operation, but provides no data for calculating or comparing actual throughput, labor savings, or per-part costs.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents a SmartLab remote-education pilot conducted from SNU in South Korea for 21 students at Arusha Technical College in Tanzania. Students remotely controlled or observed automated material-testing experiments, with GUI control and real-time 360° VR streaming. The system remained operational despite temporary network disconnections; when real-time monitoring was interrupted, recorded VR video could be replayed to review the experiment. For turnaround, SmartLab required an average of 17 minutes to handle one specimen, excluding fabrication, compared with 9 minutes for a human researcher. Despite the slower per-specimen cycle, its automation produced a theoretical monthly capacity of 664 specimens versus 252 for human researchers. The main intervention described was manual battery charging: the robot’s battery lasted eight experimental cycles, after which human researchers had to recharge it because no automatic charging dock was available. The excerpt contains no information about remote cloud-lab users submitting design-print-test jobs, the BEAR external-user pilot, or separate teleoperated test laboratories. Question: Context. We run a small cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab) with an AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2.5k, 1.5 kg payload, roughly 15 N of gripping force, wrist joint J5 limited to plus or minus 70 degrees, so no straight-down grasps near the table), SO-101 leader/follower arms, Raspberry Pi 5 wrist and fixed cameras, AprilTags, and Bambu Lab printers (two A1 mini bed-slingers with 180 mm magnetic textured-PEI plates, and an H2D). Prints are sent remotely by an AI agent after a human approval, and the agent will not send a print until a camera frame shows the plate clear; today a person removes every part. We want the arm to clear plates (first for a batch of small toys on the A1 minis in December), and later to move printed specimens into mechanical tests inside closed design-print-test loops: 3D-printed tensegrity structures under drop or compression tests, and printed fixtures for our alloy and powder workflows. A previous literature answer claimed that no publication shows an arm unloading 3D printers inside a closed experimental loop; we believe Boston University's BEAR and MAMA BEAR systems (Gongora et al. 2020, Science Advances; Snapp et al. 2024, Nature Communications) contradict this, and we also know of SmartLab (2025), TeleopLab, and commercial plate-swapping systems such as Prusa's automatic sheet changer.

Question.
(1) Which academic and industrial systems use a robot arm (or other mechanism) to remove parts from FFF/FDM printers or swap build plates? For each: the removal method (flexing a magnetic spring-steel sheet, scraping or pushing, swapping the whole plate, tilting, ejection by the print head), the printers and arms used (especially any low-cost arms), measured success rates with trial counts, cycle times, failure modes (parts stuck when warm, small or tall parts tipping, adhesion changes with plate wear), and the bed temperature or cool-down conditions that make release reliable.
(2) Closed-loop design-print-test systems with robotic specimen handling (BEAR and MAMA BEAR, SmartLab, and any others): what the arm does, how specimens reach testing machines (universal testers, compression, impact or drop rigs), throughput, uptime, human interventions or failure rates reported, and the limitations and future work their authors state.
(3) Camera-based print monitoring and verification relevant to a robot cell: detecting print failures (detachment, spaghetti, warping, layer shift) with low-cost cameras and reported accuracy; checking that the plate is clear before the next print; and automatic measurement of printed specimens (dimensions, mass, defects) before testing.
(4) Print farms with robotic tending: published throughput, uptime, human hours per print and cost per part, versus manual farms.
(5) Remote or cloud users who submit design-print-test jobs (for example BEAR's external-user pilots or teleoperated test labs): measured outcomes such as completion rate, turnaround and interventions.
(6) Given our arm's limits, which removal methods are feasible for small parts on a 180 mm bed-slinger, what forces are involved (adhesion force of PLA or PETG on textured PEI, sheet-flex force), and what is known about grasping irregular printed parts with a parallel gripper?

Prefer peer-reviewed sources from 2015 to 2026, and flag preprints, theses, and commercial or trade sources. For each claim give the DOI or URL and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.
